The thesis analyses terms of address (personal names Lirang, Inya; kin terms keklei, nak, ina, yek, arin, minie ketokek, keisi, oren, ma') in four folk tales recorded at Long Sule in July-August 2011 and gives the tales in Punan with Indonesian translation (pdf pp. 14-24, Lampiran 2). a full-text search for stress/accent tekanan/aksen/intonasi/nada/fonem/vokal/konsonan/suku kata/ejaan/lafal finds only textbook definitions ('Fonologi adalah ilmu yang mempelajari bunyi bahasa', p. 12); no orthography or pronunciation note, no stress marks.

sources.citation: Guerreiro, Antonio J. 1996. Homophony, sound changes and dialectal variations in some central Bornean languages. Mon-Khmer Studies 25: 205-226.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Kayanic (Kayan, Modang, Bahau) sound changes; Punan Aput is not a subject language. 'Punan' appears only where a Modang /c/ is suggested to be a loan from the Punan of the upper Kelai (p. 209; that is Punan Kelai, a Segai-Modang group). The sole stress-related line is Haudricourt's general remark that 'unstressed vowels /e/ are dropped' on the road to monosyllabism in Modang (p. 212). Silent on Punan Aput.
